episodes.177943: Isolated thunderstorms developed across portions of northern Illinois during the afternoon of April 19th, producing mainly large hail.
episodes.177944: Isolated thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon of April 19th.
episodes.178017: One tornado was documented that moved north out of Chase county into far southeast Morris County around 905 pm CDT.   The tornado did damage to trees and one home before ending around 3 miles south southwest of Dunlap, Kansas.  Other storms produced large hail and damaging winds.  A second line of severe storms developed after midnight during the early morning hours of April 20th and produced wind damage most concentrated in Clay County in the city of Clay Center.
episodes.178032: A warm front lifted north of the area during the early morning hours, and an approaching upper low resulted in a temperature profile that was favorable for hail development. Thunderstorms developed west of the area overnight, on the leading edge of the low level jet. These storms tracked into west central Illinois by late morning and strengthened, producing isolated large hail through early evening.
episodes.178034: Accelerated snowmelt from a near-record snowpack due to above normal temperatures produced high and fast flow on drainages in Routt County. As a result, flooding compromised some county roads and locations in Hayden, Colorado.
episodes.178125: A lone supercell thunderstorm moved from south central Kansas into central Kansas during the afternoon and evening of April 19th, 2023.  The cyclic storm produced very large hail up to 4 inches in diameter and numerous tornadoes across Chase county, Kansas.   Eight tornadoes formed from the supercell with the strongest producing EF2 damage.
episodes.178154: Broad troughing was present aloft across the Western US during the afternoon/evening of the 19th. An area of surface low-pressure slowly deepened and moved towards north-central Kansas, with dryline extending from central Kansas through western-north Texas by the late afternoon hours. A well-timed lead upper wave, combined with broken insolation, led to the development of a few supercell thunderstorms across central Oklahoma. Multiple instances of large to very large (>2 inches) hail, along with 18 tornadoes, occurred across central Oklahoma.
episodes.178179: A surge of relatively mild, moist, and unstable air aloft brought rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms to southern WI. Numerous reports of large hail were received. Flash flooding and general flooding occurred in urban areas.
episodes.178309: A line of thunderstorms produced a few gusts around 60 mph over portions of Fall River and Custer Counties.
episodes.178311: A severe thunderstorm produced wind gusts around 60 mph over portions of southern Jackson County.
episodes.178849: A deeper than average snow pack from northern Minnesota into northern Wisconsin underwent a rapid melt through much of April from unseasonably warm temperatures combined with multiple rain events. This resulted in increased water levels and significant flooding for the entire length of the local Mississippi River, with most sites climbing to their third to fifth highest crests on record. A significant mid-April rain and snow event resulted in the Governor of Wisconsin issuing a State of Emergency declaration for flooding on April 16, 2023. Initial flood warnings were issued in mid April with peak stages realized in late April. The highest above flood stage was Lynxville Dam at 5.26 ft over flood stage.
episodes.178867: Snowmelt resulted in flooding along the James River and its associated tributaries. The National Weather Service recorded an April record snow depth of 26 inches in Aberdeen on the 5th. This was followed by near normal temperatures through the latter half of the month of April. This relatively mild warmup resulted in snowmelt on top of frozen ground, and forced most of the melt into the waterways. River gauges near Columbia peaked just below major flood stage at 17.85 feet on April 30th and near Stratford just below moderate flood stage with 16.75 feet on April 30th. The gauge near Ashton peaked well above major flood stage at 19.91 feet on April 21st, which overtopped one of the bridges and impacted another near the gauge site. The gauge near Redfield peaked at 22.3 feet on April 22nd, just above moderate flood stage. Aside from the bridges and a few roads that were impacted, the main result of this high water was flooding of agricultural lands.
episodes.178894: A cold front moved across eastern Nebraska which had observed unseasonably warm temperatures in the past couple of days. The front set off a line of storms that produced strong wind gusts and large hail. The strongest measured wind gust was 67 mph in Sarpy County and there were several 1.75-inch hail reports in Otoe County. A flash flood was reported in Sarpy County as 2-3 inches of rain fell across the county.
episodes.179012: Much of the Elm River drainage basin experienced a cold slow start to spring, leaving the ground frozen when temperatures finally started to consistently warm above freezing during the second week in April. Snow water equivalent at the start of April was in excess of 4 inches, with most of the melt entering waterways and the resultant flooding mainly affecting agricultural lands.||A Presidential Disaster Declaration was approved for Brown, Clark, Codington, Day, Faulk, Grant, Hand, Marshall, Potter and Roberts Counties, as well as for the Lake Traverse Indian Reservation, where an estimated $2,305,362 in total qualifying costs were incurred during spring flooding.
episodes.179013: Early morning storms associated with a weakening low resulted in one stronger cell in central Iowa producing quarter sized hail before dawn. Later in the day, a deepening low across the central plains lifted into Iowa with storms developing along a dry line in the evening. These storms produced hail up to baseball sized, along with a brief tornado remained rural and did not cause any damage. Additional convection was reinvigorated overnight thanks to the low level et, but remained sub severe. Areas that received multiple rounds of storms saw two to three inches of much needed rain.
episodes.179142: On this Tuesday late afternoon and evening, thunderstorms of varying strength rumbled from southwest-to-northeast across portions of South Central Nebraska mainly between 6:00-11:30 p.m. CDT. However, the vast majority of strong to severe activity focused within a 15-30 mile wide swath centered along a line from Franklin-Blue Hill-Sutton-York. Within this corridor, there were a number of reports of large hail ranging from quarter size up to tennis ball size, with the tennis ball (2.5 inch) reports out of Harvard and Stockham. There were also several instances of ping pong ball to golf ball size stones, including in or near the following communities: Blue Hill, Sutton, Edgar and Glenvil. Finally, marginally-severe, quarter to half dollar size hail reports originated from in or near places such as: Franklin, Bladen, Clay Center, Deweese and York. Large hail was clearly the main story of the evening, as there were only a few measured strong to marginally-severe gusts of 50+ MPH, a few of which were several miles removed from obvious thunderstorm outflow and were likely associated with a weak wake low. A few of the strongest detected gusts included 58 MPH in Doniphan (unofficial mesonet) and ASOS-measured gusts of 55 and 52 MPH at Grand Island and Hastings airports, respectively. ||Breaking down event evolution/timing, if anything the intensity of storms (and peak hail size) ended up being a bit surprising given the seasonably-modest and just in time nature of low-level moisture advecting northward into the area along a slow-moving surface warm front. At daybreak on the 18th, this west-east oriented front was aligned across northern Kansas, with South Central Nebraska firmly on its cool/dry side with surface dewpoints mainly only in the 20s (F). Meanwhile, in the mid-upper levels, the Central Plains resided well downstream of a large scale trough centered over the Northern Rockies. Over the course of the day, a subtle wave along the leading edges of the aforementioned parent trough entered the Central High Plains. This prompted a gradual increase in west-southwesterly, mid-upper level flow into South Central Nebraska, along with a gradual increase in south-southeasterly low-level flow, allowing slow-but-steady northward moisture transport into the lifting warm frontal zone. By late afternoon (around the time of convective initiation), a 994 millibar surface low was noted over northwest Kansas, with the attendant warm front extending into far southern Nebraska to its east, and a north-south oriented dryline trailing southward. Although still seasonably-unimpressive, surface dewpoints over the southern half of South Central Nebraska had risen well into the mid-upper 40s by this time (a surge of nearly 20 degrees over early morning values). This meager-but-sufficient low level moisture, combined with steep low-to-mid level lapse rates and convergence near the warm front/dryline intersection, was enough to initiate the first high-based storms of the afternoon over north central Kansas around 5:30 p.m. CDT. Already by 6 p.m. CDT, the first severe-warned storm of the day within South Central Nebraska had entered southern Franklin County. During the next two hours, a series of semi-discrete, strong-to-severe cells affected primarily Franklin/Webster counties. Then, between 8-10 p.m. CDT, intense elevated convection consolidated into a more cohesive line as it tracked northeastward across portions of mainly Adams/Clay/Nuckolls/Hamilton/Fillmore counties, aided by an uptick in a 40-50 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). Finally, between 10:00-11:30 p.m. CDT, this severe storm complex traversed York County before exiting the local area into eastern Nebraska, while other non-severe cells passed through various counties mainly along/north of Highway 92 before also departing South Central Nebraska...thus ending all local thunderstorm activity for the night. As it turned out, despite the unimpressive low level moisture magnitude, the combination of mixed-layer CAPE increasing to as high as 1000-1500 J/kg during the evening, combined with strong effective deep-layer wind shear around 50 knots, proved plenty sufficient to ignite robust updrafts.
episodes.179202: There was a both a marginal risk for severe weather and excessive rainfall. Discrete storms developed near 10 PM and produced several hail reports and a couple of wind reports in Cass County. Additionally, a flash flood was observed in Fremont.
episodes.179217: An enhanced risk resulted in a widespread large hail event across southeast Nebraska. Storms developed after 4 PM along a stationary front near the Nebraska/Kansas border. A total of 55 storm reports were sent out by the office, most of which were for hail. The largest hailstone reported was 3 inches near Nebraska City. In addition to the hail, there were 4 observed tornadoes in OAX's Iowa counties.
episodes.179221: An enhanced risk resulted in a numerous hail event across southwest Iowa. Storms developed after 4 PM along a stationary front near the Nebraska/Kansas border and moved into Iowa. A total of 55 storm reports were sent out by the office, most of which were for hail. The largest hailstone reported was 3 inches near Thurman. In addition to the hail, there were 3 observed tornadoes. Two in Fremont County and one in Pottawatomie County.
episodes.179431: Heavy rainfall was able to close some roads across the eastern half of the state.
episodes.179481: Thunderstorms during the early morning hours produced high winds over Brown and Day Counties. The highest observed wind gust was 78 mph 5 miles south-southeast of Pierpont. A 65 mph gust was reported 4 miles northwest of Pierpont. A cooperative observer in Faulkton reported small hail.
episodes.179753: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the morning hours of April 19th. These showers and storms developed along a cold front that moved across eastern Iowa. Some of these storms became severe north of US Highway 30, and produced hail up to the size of golf balls.
episodes.179758: Scattered thunderstorms developed in far northwest Illinois during the afternoon hours as a cold front moved into western Illinois. These storms intensified as they moved into Bureau County and produced hail up to the size of golf balls.
episodes.179767: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the Nebraska Panhandle during the early evening hours of April 18th. As this activity tracked into the northeastern Nebraska Panhandle and northwestern Sandhills, gusty winds were reported. Thunderstorm wind gusts to 65 MPH were reported at Rushville.
episodes.180044: Snowmelt flooding along the North Dakota Tributaries began in early to mid-April, with a few locations persisting into early May.
episodes.180161: A weak upper-level wave moving through southwest flow aloft, acting on an environment with 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MUCAPE in the vicinity of a surface trough, resulted in scattered thunderstorms across far southeast South Dakota, far northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota during the evening of April 19th. The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
episodes.180165: A weak upper-level wave moving through southwest flow aloft, acting on an environment with 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MUCAPE in the vicinity of a surface trough, resulted in scattered thunderstorms across far southeast South Dakota, far northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, and southwest Minnesota during the evening of April 19th. The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
